primary_source_citation.title: FEMA National Preparedness Goal Technical Reference: The Five Phases of Emergency Management (FEMA Framework)

1.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Emergency management operates as a continuous five-mission cycle of Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery.
core_mechanism_bullets: 1. Prevention & Mitigation (Before): Eliminate or reduce hazard impact ahead of time: smoke/CO alarms, strapping water heaters, clearing storm drains.
2. Preparedness & Family Drills (Before): Build 72-hour Go-Bags, designate an out-of-state phone relay contact, and practice two exit routes per room.
3. Immediate Response (During Crisis): Protect life safety first, account for all family and patrol members via buddy system, and avoid downed lines.
4. Short & Long-Term Recovery (After): Restore utilities safely, document damage with photos, check on elderly neighbors, and debrief lessons learned.
1.worked_field_example: Clearing dry brush 30 feet around a cabin is Mitigation, packing a 72-hour Go-Bag is Preparedness, and evacuating early is Response.
1.counselor_tabletop_demo: Walk a wildfire or flood scenario around all five segments of the preparedness wheel to identify one Scout action in each phase.
1.real_world_connection_box: FEMA National Preparedness Goal Field Standard: Emergency management operates as a continuous five-mission cycle of Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery.
1.grounded_citation_label: Verified: Scouting America Pamphlet + FEMA National Preparedness Goal (PPD-8)
1.bespoke_visual_caption: Five-part circular preparedness emblem illustrating Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery.

2.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Emergency management operates as a continuous five-mission cycle of Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery.
core_mechanism_bullets: Incident Commander (Single Point of Command): Sets overall incident objectives, safety priorities, and coordinates directly with fire, police, and EMS.
Safety Officer (Authority to Stop Unsafe Acts): Continuously monitors scene hazards, heat/cold stress, hydration, and strict Scouting Youth Protection.
Operations & Logistics Sections: Operations runs safe Scout support tasks (shelter canteen, runner messages); Logistics manages gear, food, radios.
Planning & Check-In Accountability: Maintains written roster check-in/check-out logs so every Scout and volunteer is accounted for every hour.
2.worked_field_example: Clearing dry brush 30 feet around a cabin is Mitigation, packing a 72-hour Go-Bag is Preparedness, and evacuating early is Response.

primary_source_citation.title: FEMA Ready.gov & American Red Cross Technical Reference: Safe Rescue Hierarchy & Utility Emergency Shutoff Rules

3.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Always follow the low-to-high-risk rescue sequence of Reach, Throw, Row, and Go with training and flotation so a rescuer never becomes a second victim.
core_mechanism_bullets: Reach - Throw - Row - Go Ladder: Always extend a pole/branch or throw a buoyant line from shore first before committing a trained rescuer.
Downed Power Lines (35+ Foot Rule): Treat every fallen wire as energized; keep back at least 35 feet and shuffle feet together without lifting.
Natural Gas & Carbon Monoxide: Rotten-egg mercaptan odor or CO alarm: evacuate outdoors immediately without touching switches; call 911 outside.
72-Hour Go-Kit Core Standard: 1 gallon of water per person per day (3 gal total), non-perishable food, headlamp, NOAA radio, first aid, meds.
3.worked_field_example: When a victim falls through dock water 8 feet from shore, lie flat on the dock and extend a paddle or throw a buoyant ring before entering the water.
3.counselor_tabletop_demo: Practice coiling and heaving a rescue throw-bag line to a target marker 25 feet away while keeping both feet anchored on dry ground.
3.real_world_connection_box: American Red Cross Lifesaving Hierarchy Standard: Always follow the low-to-high-risk rescue sequence of Reach, Throw, Row, and Go with training and flotation so a rescuer never becomes a second victim.
3.grounded_citation_label: Verified: Scouting America Pamphlet + American Red Cross Rescue Hierarchy
3.bespoke_visual_caption: Four-panel rescue progression illustrating extending a branch from shore, heaving a throw-bag, approaching by boat, and tethered PFD swimming.
3.v47_slide_title: American Red Cross Lifesaving Hierarchy Standard
v47_primary_source_bullets: Always follow the low-to-high-risk rescue sequence of Reach, Throw, Row, and Go with training and flotation so a rescuer never becomes a second victim.

primary_source_citation.title: NASAR & National Park Service SAR Technical Reference: Backcountry Lost-Person Search & Rescue (SAR) Containment

4.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Always follow the low-to-high-risk rescue sequence of Reach, Throw, Row, and Go with training and flotation so a rescuer never becomes a second victim.
core_mechanism_bullets: Phase 1: Freeze Point Last Seen (PLS): Flag the exact spot and time the missing person was last seen so boot tracks and scent clues stay undisturbed.
Phase 2: Containment & Hasty Teams: Post lookouts at trail junctions, road crossings, and creek bridges while fast teams check high-probability trails.
Phase 3: High-Probability Clue Search: Searchers look for physical clues (footprints, wrapper, broken twigs) because clues outnumber people 100 to 1.
Phase 4: Safe Scout Mobilization Boundaries: Scouts serve in supervised base-camp logistics, communications, and perimeter support within council safety rules.
4.worked_field_example: When a victim falls through dock water 8 feet from shore, lie flat on the dock and extend a paddle or throw a buoyant ring before entering the water.
4.counselor_tabletop_demo: Practice coiling and heaving a rescue throw-bag line to a target marker 25 feet away while keeping both feet anchored on dry ground.
4.real_world_connection_box: American Red Cross Lifesaving Hierarchy Standard: Always follow the low-to-high-risk rescue sequence of Reach, Throw, Row, and Go with training and flotation so a rescuer never becomes a second victim.

6.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Incident Command organizes every response into five clear sections of Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance.
core_mechanism_bullets: Incident Commander (Single Point of Command): Sets overall incident objectives, safety priorities, and coordinates directly with fire, police, and EMS.
Safety Officer (Authority to Stop Unsafe Acts): Continuously monitors scene hazards, heat/cold stress, hydration, and strict Scouting Youth Protection.
Operations & Logistics Sections: Operations runs safe Scout support tasks (shelter canteen, runner messages); Logistics manages gear, food, radios.
Planning & Check-In Accountability: Maintains written roster check-in/check-out logs so every Scout and volunteer is accounted for every hour.
6.worked_field_example: During a 25-Scout camp mobilization, five patrol leaders report to one Operations Chief rather than all 25 Scouts reporting to one adult.
6.counselor_tabletop_demo: Assign five Scouts to the five color-coded ICS section roles (Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance) for a simulated camp storm drill.
6.real_world_connection_box: FEMA NIMS & ICS-100 Incident Command Standard: Incident Command organizes every response into five clear sections of Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance. Maintain a manageable span of control of three to seven personnel per supervisor with five as the optimum ratio.

7.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Anchor every lost-person response by flagging the Point Last Seen and establishing a containment perimeter before starting grid sweeps.
core_mechanism_bullets: Reach - Throw - Row - Go Ladder: Always extend a pole/branch or throw a buoyant line from shore first before committing a trained rescuer.
Downed Power Lines (35+ Foot Rule): Treat every fallen wire as energized; keep back at least 35 feet and shuffle feet together without lifting.
Natural Gas & Carbon Monoxide: Rotten-egg mercaptan odor or CO alarm: evacuate outdoors immediately without touching switches; call 911 outside.
72-Hour Go-Kit Core Standard: 1 gallon of water per person per day (3 gal total), non-perishable food, headlamp, NOAA radio, first aid, meds.
7.worked_field_example: Posting lookouts on trails and streams within a 1-mile radius of the Point Last Seen keeps a wandering hiker inside the search box.
7.counselor_tabletop_demo: Mark a Point Last Seen on a topo map and lay out a 360-degree containment boundary before assigning parallel hasty-search teams.
